:::{#def-nullity}
#### Nullity

The **nullity** of a matrix $\matr{A}$ is
the dimension of its null space (@def-null-space):

$$
\operatorname{nullity}(\matr{A}) \eqdef \dim\paren{\mathcal{N}(\matr{A})}.
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-nullity}
#### The nullity of the matrix in @exm-column-space

For $\matr{A}$ in @exm-column-space,
$\mathcal{N}(\matr{A}) = \operatorname{span}\cb{(2, 1, 0), (2, 0, 1)}$
(@exm-null-space).
Those two vectors are linearly independent:
$c_1 (2, 1, 0) + c_2 (2, 0, 1) = (2c_1 + 2c_2, c_1, c_2)$,
which is $\vzero_3$ only if $c_1 = c_2 = 0$.
So they are a basis of $\mathcal{N}(\matr{A})$,
and $\operatorname{nullity}(\matr{A}) = 2$.
The $2 \times 2$ identity matrix has nullity $0$,
because $\matr{I} \vecf{x} = \vecf{x}$ is $\vzero_2$ only when $\vecf{x} = \vzero_2$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-rank-nullity}
#### Rank-nullity theorem

For any $m \times n$ matrix $\matr{A}$,

$$
\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}) + \operatorname{nullity}(\matr{A}) = n.
$$

:::

::: proof

Let $\nu = \operatorname{nullity}(\matr{A})$.
Choose a basis $\vecf{x}_1, \ldots, \vecf{x}_\nu$ of $\mathcal{N}(\matr{A})$,
and extend it to a basis
$\vecf{x}_1, \ldots, \vecf{x}_\nu, \vecf{y}_1, \ldots, \vecf{y}_{n - \nu}$
of $\reals^n$ (@thm-extend-basis);
it has $n$ vectors,
because every basis of $\reals^n$ has $\dim(\reals^n) = n$ vectors
(@thm-basis-size, @exm-dimension).
We show that $\matr{A} \vecf{y}_1, \ldots, \matr{A} \vecf{y}_{n - \nu}$
are a basis of $\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$,
using @thm-matvec-linear to apply $\matr{A}$ to linear combinations.

**They are linearly independent.**
Suppose $\sum_{i=1}^{n-\nu} v_i\,\matr{A} \vecf{y}_i = \vzero_m$.
Then $\matr{A}\,\paren{\sum_i v_i \vecf{y}_i} = \vzero_m$ (@thm-matvec-linear),
so $\sum_i v_i \vecf{y}_i \in \mathcal{N}(\matr{A})$,
and it equals $\sum_{j=1}^{\nu} u_j \vecf{x}_j$ for some numbers $u_j$,
since the $\vecf{x}_j$ span $\mathcal{N}(\matr{A})$.
Moving everything to one side,

$$
\sum_{j=1}^{\nu} (-u_j)\,\vecf{x}_j + \sum_{i=1}^{n-\nu} v_i \vecf{y}_i = \vzero_n,
$$

and because the $\vecf{x}$'s and $\vecf{y}$'s together form a basis of $\reals^n$,
which is linearly independent,
every coefficient is $0$; in particular every $v_i = 0$.

**They span $\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$.**
Take any $\vecf{w} \in \mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$,
so $\vecf{w} = \matr{A} \vecf{z}$ for some $\vecf{z} \in \reals^n$
(@def-column-space).
Write $\vecf{z} = \sum_j a_j \vecf{x}_j + \sum_i b_i \vecf{y}_i$
in the basis of $\reals^n$.
Then

$$
\ba
\vecf{w}
&= \matr{A}\,\paren{\sum_{j=1}^{\nu} a_j \vecf{x}_j + \sum_{i=1}^{n-\nu} b_i \vecf{y}_i}
&& \text{(substitute } \vecf{z} \text{)}
\\
&= \sum_{j=1}^{\nu} a_j\,\matr{A} \vecf{x}_j + \sum_{i=1}^{n-\nu} b_i\,\matr{A} \vecf{y}_i
&& \text{(@thm-matvec-linear)}
\\
&= \sum_{j=1}^{\nu} a_j\,\vzero_m + \sum_{i=1}^{n-\nu} b_i\,\matr{A} \vecf{y}_i
&& \text{(each } \vecf{x}_j \in \mathcal{N}(\matr{A}) \text{)}
\\
&= \sum_{i=1}^{n-\nu} b_i\,\matr{A} \vecf{y}_i,
&& \text{(drop the zero terms)}
\ea
$$

a linear combination of $\matr{A} \vecf{y}_1, \ldots, \matr{A} \vecf{y}_{n-\nu}$.
These vectors are in $\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$,
so their span is exactly $\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$.

So $\dim\paren{\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})} = n - \nu$,
and $\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}) = n - \nu$ by @thm-rank-dim.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-rank-nullity}
#### Checking rank-nullity on the matrix in @exm-column-space

The matrix $\matr{A}$ in @exm-column-space has $n = 3$ columns,
rank $1$ (@exm-rank-dim)
and nullity $2$ (@exm-nullity),
and $1 + 2 = 3$.
The $2 \times 2$ identity matrix has rank $2$ and nullity $0$ (@exm-nullity),
and $2 + 0 = 2$.

:::
